text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Lower Saxony premier Gerhard Schroeder, speaking at an "innovation congress" organised by the Social Democrats, supports proposal from DGB union leaders on pensions and wages.

- VEBA buys 36.4 percent of Degussa for 2.91 billion marks. VEBA will thus become largest shareholder in Degussa, but company management and VEBA are in agreement over continuing company's current strategies.
- Opponents of nuclear waste dump in Gorleben see new hopes after Berlin administration court supports challenge of lower course decision by foes of the waste dump.
- Young leaders of centrist Free Democrats warn FDP not to met CDU halfway and accept tax increases.
HANDELSBLATT
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl is still unsatisfied with German industry's support for Expo 2000 in Hanover. He tells newspaper in interview that their support has to increase dramatically.
- French ITM Intermarche Enterprises takes indirect stake in Spar-Handels AG of Schneenefeld near Hamburg.
- VEBA to become largest shareholder in Degussa.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG

- SPD wants to thoroughly modernise jobs and industry in Germany. Party leaders meet in Duesseldorf. SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine demands new partnership between labour and capital and criticises Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government for slow pace of reform. Germany should become a high-tech country and recapture its international competitiveness.

- Finance Minster Theo Waigel wants to give federal and state ministries more control of their own budgets -- giving them more responsiblity as well. Waigel hopes to save millions of marks in this fashion.
- Federal support for "Aufbau Ost" programme to rebuild eastern German will continue until at least 1999, Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt says.
DIE WELT
- Opponents of Morsleben nuclear dump win round in Berlin court.
- Schroeder welcomes proposals by DGB leader Schulte on pensions and more flexible wages.
- VEBA will acquire stake in Degussa for 2.9 billion marks.
- Postbank has a 1996 deficit of 1.256 billion marks due to unexpected high costs.
- Federal cartel office critical of sale of Berlin utility BEWAG to German-American consortium.
